summary: Proposes the Voice File Interchange Protocol (VFIP), a way to exchange speech files between different systems in the ARPA-Internet community. It is an early proposal that invites suggestions for improvement rather than a finished standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 978 proposes a header that describes a speech file so different systems can identify its format and recording details. The header can travel with the speech data or be stored separately.

questions: how to exchange voice files between computers
what encoding methods does vfip support
what does the vfip header contain
subtitle: A header format for exchanging speech files between different systems.

tldr.problem: Speech systems use different formats, making voice files difficult to exchange and convert between systems.
tldr.mechanism: VFIP adds an 18-byte header describing the file's version, length, DTMF tones, recording rate, duration, and encoding method.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes a common way to describe speech data and says the header may be stored with the audio or in a separate associated file.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 978's status as Unknown. The RFC describes VFIP as a proposed format and encourages suggestions for improvement.

sections.title: Describing Different Speech Formats
sections.content:
The Voice File Interchange Protocol (VFIP) aims to let different systems exchange speech files. The RFC says there was growing interest in voice, including multimedia mail, but no specific standard focused on compatibility among voice implementations.

VFIP defines a header that describes voice data. The description can help another system interpret the file and support conversion between formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Different systems need a shared description to interpret each other's speech files. VFIP proposes a header that carries that description.

sections.title: Fields in the VFIP Header
sections.content:
The header is 18 bytes for version one. It contains a one-byte version number and a one-byte header length, followed by a 16-bit DTMF mask, a 32-bit approximate recording rate, a 32-bit total time in deci-seconds, and a six-byte encoding or recording method name.

In the DTMF mask, a set bit guarantees that its corresponding tone is absent; a clear bit means the tone may or may not occur. The method name is compared without regard to letter case and shorter names are padded with spaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The header records how the speech was encoded, its approximate data rate, its duration, and what is known about touch-tones. The DTMF bits say which tones are definitely absent.

sections.title: How the Header Relates to Speech Data
sections.content:
VFIP's header does not have to be placed at the start of the speech file. It may instead be kept in a separate file associated with the speech data.

The RFC illustrates the format with a one-minute, 2400-bits-per-second NVP-2 recording and a ten-second, 1200-bits-per-second TI recording. In the second example, the DTMF mask guarantees that tones 0 through 9 are absent but does not describe the other tones.
sections.plainLanguage: The description can be stored alongside the audio or in a separate associated file. The examples show how the header records a file's method, rate, duration, and known tones.
